prompt: Use case: ui-mockup. Create one high-fidelity desktop web app lesson-player screen, landscape 16:10, edge-to-edge, crisp readable English UI, no device mockup or outer caption. This is a design proposal, not implementation. Product: HISTORY, an interactive history learning app. Same sample chapter in every alternative: The Silk Roads / At the crossroads, chapter 2 of 5. The attached reference contributes ONLY the Worlds identity: inky navy, rich plum, warm ivory, restrained amber controls, classical editorial lettering, luminous historical illustrations. Do not copy its three-phone layout or reuse its art as wallpaper. Preserve compact navigation: HISTORY, Chapters, bookmark, Sources, sound. Bottom controls: Previous, a five-part chapter progress indicator, Next. Narration is optional and user-paced: show Read / Listen, play/pause and seek; Next remains usable while audio plays. Visible prose must teach real history, not give instructions about the UI. No quiz, radio choices, scores, fake citations, generic card dashboard, oversized slogan, giant empty header, or essay hidden below the viewport. Generated historical imagery is visibly labeled Reconstruction; map routes schematic. Composition: an expansive cartographic learning instrument, not a hero image. A textured, geographically plausible Eurasian atlas with coastlines and terrain is the dominant surface, ink-blue sea and dark muted earth with readable amber route segments. Label only Chang’an, Dunhuang, Samarkand and Constantinople; do not invent political boundaries. Samarkand is the selected junction. A magnified painted city vignette is anchored naturally beside that location, not a floating generic card. Overlapping paths and arrows show a relay of exchanges; a compact artifact trail displays a silk bolt, paper sheet and manuscript, with Paper selected. A bottom integrated reading band holds heading “Ideas travelled by relay” and two legible paragraphs: “The Silk Roads were a network, not a single road. Merchants could carry goods along one section, sell them, and leave the next journey to someone else.” “Skills travelled with people too. Papermaking spread across regions over centuries; the movement of a technique depended on craftspeople and local workshops, not just a sheet arriving at a market.” A small timeline with “Move along the network” handles changes the map’s illustrated stage. Show “Schematic connections · different centuries” clearly. Evidence button: “Read how paper spread”. The learner’s focus is the network and changing historical explanation, no mandatory route puzzle. Rich visual cartography, intentional typography, ample reading size, one calm cohesive screen.
purpose: Lesson-player composition proposal; illustrative artwork and unverified generated map/chronology labels.
approval: User 2026-11-22: likes all four, including spatial exploration; build a fluid system using these references.
